## Act I: The Ghost {.center .folio background-color="#f5efe1"}

### *Something is rotten in the state of Denmark*

::: {.notes}
(Act card. The title of this talk is a Hamlet joke, so we may as well commit: five acts.)

## {background-image="img/kermit-typing.gif"}

::: {.notes}

Last year, we found ourselves getting more and more into using Claude Code. One of the great things about our current moment in the industry is that so many things that may have seemed hard or out of reach before are now available for us to do. It lets us be much more responsive to new ideas and requests--now we can just fire off Claude on a git worktree without having to do all of the context switching to consider it, and many times it just gets it done, or pretty close. 
:::

## {background-image="img/kermit-thinking-cropped.jpg"}

::: {.notes}
So, increasingly, I kept seeing problems and thinking, how can I use Claude to solve it? What else out there have we learned to be hard and painful that maybe isn't anymore?
:::

## {background-image="img/kermit-phone.gif"}

::: {.notes}
Responding to support escalations became one of them. Posit uses Zendesk for support, customers can file tickets there and they get fielded by our support team. When they get a clear bug report, or something that they can't answer on their own, it escalates to the engineers.

I thought, Claude is good at reading the codebase, developing an understanding of how it works, and pinpointing bugs. But when fielding a support escalation, a human engineer still has to read the full Zendesk ticket history, sometimes download and extract server diagnostics that were uploaded, and synthesize that. How can I just plug Zendesk into Claude and let it figure it out?

I want to just take the ticket URL and give it to Claude Code like this:
:::

:::{.notes}
The first piece is authentication--I can't provide my credentials to connect to the Zendesk API. But even if I could, I would run into other challenges: the Zendesk REST API is not designed for AI agents to make efficient and secure use of it.

## MCP is designed to solve this {.center}

### [space]{.ghost}

::: {.notes}
MCP offers a solution to this. 

It provides a way for you to authenticate securely to APIs, without giving your credentials to the agent. 

By writing a custom MCP server, you can control exactly what tools are made available and what capabilities they expose. This improves your agent's performance, and it also allows you to protect against a range of security vulnerabilties.

And by hosting an MCP server, you can easily share it with others. 

So today I'm going to talk about MCP, what it's good for and what it's less suited for, and some best practices from my experience. When it's the right tool for the job, MCP can unlock superpowers for your agentic workflows. And when done well, it can actually improve your security posture, which is especially important for AI agents.

A central point I want to land, and that really underlies everything in the talk:
:::

## You can write and host your own MCP servers {.center}

### [https://github.com/nealrichardson/zendesk-mcp-server]{.ghost}

::: {.epigraph}
This above all: to thine own self be true
:::

:::{.notes}
To do exactly what you need. Because code is now cheap. So my talk is going to be oriented about writing your own, not about whether or not you should use an MCP server that someone else provides. Even when someone else's hosted MCP server is available to you, you may have reasons for wanting to customize it, as I will show. And thanks to AI, this is all available to you now.
:::

## Act II: What's in a Name? {.center .folio background-color="#f5efe1"}

### *That which we call a rose<br>by any other name would smell as sweet*

::: {.notes}
Act II: what this thing actually is.

Juliet's argument is that a name has put a barrier between her and something that is plainly right there. That's this act. "MCP" sounds like a new discipline you have to go learn. Strip the name off it and it's an HTTP API with a schema for describing functions, and you already know how to build and serve those.
:::

## What is MCP? {.center}

::: {.notes}
first want to say what it is not
:::

## MCP is specification for providing tools to LLMs

![](img/ikea.png)


:::{.notes}
* Tools: functions that LLMs can call, the model "sees" that function exists, with a description telling it what it does, what the inputs are, and what the outputs are.

* MCP defines a standard for servers that host tools, and how to register them in your client, any AI application
:::

## Local vs. Remote MCP

### Local

* Runs on your machine
* `claude mcp add name-here -- uvx --from "git+https://github.com/user/repo"`
* Can access your local file system etc.

## Local vs. Remote MCP

### Local

* Runs on your machine
* `claude mcp add name-here -- uvx --from "git+https://github.com/user/repo"`
* Can access your local file system etc.

### Remote

* Runs somewhere else
* `claude mcp add --transport http name-here https://example.com/mcp`
* **Cannot** access your local file system but can access whatever you give the server

:::{.notes}
For a few reasons, I'm going to focus on remote MCP, and in particular on remote MCP servers that you write to do exactly what you need. I think this is the use case that has the most real value today.
:::

## MCP is an API standard {.center}

:::{.notes}
* It's a standard for how to design APIs that AI applications can use

* Remote MCP servers communicate over HTTP, basically JSON RPC with a set of well known endpoints and a schema for how tools are defined. 

* Realizing that MCP was just a convention for how to set up API endpoints helped demystify it for me. As someone who has worked in software and data for many years, I know how to use an HTTP API, I know how to build and serve them too. 
:::

## {background-image="img/unix-system.jpg"}

::: {.notes}
You know what this is too. And your coding agents do too.

## I come to bury MCP, not to praise him {.folio}

![](img/mcp-is-dead.png)

https://uxplanet.org/mcp-is-dead-cf16b667ba6d

::: {.notes}
Antony, over Caesar's body. He says "I come to bury Caesar, not to praise him" and then spends the whole speech turning the crowd back around. Which is what I'm about to do, so it's fair to tell you now.

The Forum scene is also the best picture anyone has of a hype cycle: a crowd swung hard one way and then hard the other, by rhetoric rather than by any new facts.

Like most things, there is truth in both the initial excitement for MCP and the hard backlash against it. There weren't good alternatives to MCP when it came out, so people used it for all kinds of things and in questionable ways that today don't make sense. It's ideal for some use cases, and for others you are better off using a CLI. 

Critiques

* Best tool for the job

* Inherent risks with agentic AI

* Best practices

:::

## MCP, CLI, or Skill?

* If the agent can do everything with tools it already has (Bash, Fetch, etc.) then a Skill is probably enough

* Otherwise, Skill is complement: we're talking (MCP + Skill) vs. (CLI + Skill)

## Words, words, words {.center .folio background-color="#f5efe1"}

### Every tool definition is loaded up front, whether you use it or not

::: {.notes}
Polonius asks Hamlet what he's reading. "Words, words, words."

That's the context critique in three words: it all goes in, it all costs tokens, and most of it is not what you're here for.
:::

## (MCP + Skill) vs. (CLI + Skill)

::: {.columns}

:::: {.column width="40%"}
![](img/Two-Buttons.jpg)
::::

:::: {.column width="60%"}

Critique that MCP takes up too much context: all tool definitions are loaded up front and take up tokens

Claude Code is good with CLIs: why use GitHub's MCP if `gh` is already right there?

Use CLI when:

* CLI already exists, is widely available and in the training data

* Your agent has Bash available to call the CLI
::::
:::

:::{.notes}
CLI not and option if the AI application can't run shell commands
:::

## Things a CLI cannot do for you

* Authenticate on your behalf, without handing the agent your credentials

* Reach resources your machine can't

* Get added by URL, in one command

:::{.notes}
So that's the case for the CLI. Here's what it can't do, and this is where remote MCP earns its place.

A CLI runs as you, with your credentials, on your machine. If the thing you need is behind an auth boundary, or simply isn't reachable from your laptop, the CLI has nowhere to go. And distributing one means everybody installs and authenticates it out of band, where a remote server is a single command with a URL.

Which is the answer to the question this act asked. Hold onto it: in Act V I'll show you it actually working.
:::

## Act IV: Something Wicked This Way Comes {.center .folio background-color="#f5efe1"}

### *Oftentimes, to win us to our harm,<br>the instruments of darkness tell us truths*

::: {.notes}
Act IV: the danger, and then the discipline.

Banquo, on the witches. The word that matters is *instruments* — tools. Note what he doesn't say: he doesn't say they lie to you. Macbeth is destroyed by prophecies that all come true. No man of woman born; Birnam Wood will never move. Every one of them accurate, and every one of them fatal, because someone else chose which truths he got to hear.

That is the failure mode. Not a tool that lies. A tool that returns nothing but true things, and takes you somewhere you would never have gone.
:::

## Double, double, toil and trouble {.folio background-color="#f5efe1"}

### The lethal trifecta

* Access to private data

* Exposure to untrusted content

* Ability to exfiltrate

https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/

:::{.notes}
"If your agent combines these three features, an attacker can easily trick it into accessing your private data and sending it to that attacker."

The reason this is a cauldron and not a list: no single one of these is a vulnerability. Reading private data is your job. Reading a GitHub issue is your job. Sending a web request is your job. Each ingredient is inert. It's the combining that conjures something, and that's the part people miss when they audit these one at a time.

Not specific to MCP, either — but there were some very public examples in the early months of MCP.
:::

## Look like the innocent flower,<br>but be the serpent under't {.center .folio background-color="#f5efe1"}

### A prompt injection, disguised as a GitHub issue

::: {.notes}
Lady Macbeth, coaching her husband on how to host a murder.

It's not just that the MCP server itself may be malicious. Suppose you're reading GitHub issues on a public repo — whether with GitHub's MCP server or the `gh` CLI, doesn't matter. Someone writes a prompt injection into an issue. That's ingredient two, and it arrived looking like ordinary work.

Presumably you're already doing something with private data, so that's two. And if your agent has any tool at all that can send data outward, you have all three, and you assembled it yourself out of three reasonable decisions.

(This is the character from the cast list. It has been waiting since the beginning.)
:::

## Suit the action to the word,<br>the word to the action {.center .folio background-color="#f5efe1"}

### [space]{.ghost}

::: {.notes}
So: the counter-spell.

Hamlet's advice-to-the-players speech is, genuinely, a best practices list — a guy telling working professionals how to do their job, at length, unprompted. So I'm in good company.

And these are mostly about the cauldron. Every one of them is a way of not putting an ingredient in.
:::

## Best practices {.center}

### 1. Only define the tools you need

:::{.notes}
To reiterate, I'm talking about writing and deploying your own remote MCP servers

One reason is for efficiency:

Every tool definition consumes context in your agent. That's tokens. Both money and distraction from what your real question is. 

So, unlike when you're making a REST API to interact with via other software, or a web app, or whatever, you want a small number of tools that do exactly what you want. Any more than that has a cost.

Another reason is security: do you really need tools that can write?

If the answer is "sometimes", make more than one server, or make it configurable and make different deployments, or have some other means of allowing users of your MCP server to select only what they need?
:::

## Best practices {.center}

### 2. Make responses concise

:::{.notes}
Brevity is the soul of wit. Which, in the play, is said by...
:::

## {.center .folio background-color="#f5efe1"}

> My liege, and madam, to expostulate<br>
> What majesty should be, what duty is,<br>
> Why day is day, night night, and time is time,<br>
> Were nothing but to waste night, day, and time.<br>
> Therefore, since **brevity is the soul of wit**,<br>
> And tediousness the limbs and outward flourishes,<br>
> I will be brief.

::: {.attribution}
— Polonius, taking 43 words to say "I will be brief"
:::

:::{.notes}
The joke in the play is that the man who says "brevity is the soul of wit" is the most tedious character in it. He cannot get to the point.

This is every API response you are about to pipe into your agent's context window.
:::

## More matter, with less art {.center .folio background-color="#f5efe1"}

### [Gertrude, cutting him off]{.ghost}

::: {.notes}
Gertrude's reply. Cut him off mid-flourish. That is the design principle.

When you're working with an API that's designed for developers to work with, or web apps to build on, the API responses for a given record can include lots of details. And that makes sense when you're a (human) developer, you can select out the bits you want and ignore the rest.

But with LLMs, everything you return goes into the context. Again, that's more tokens, and more confusion. So we want to scope our MCP tools to only return the pieces that matter for the task you're asking the agent to do.

For example, in the Zendesk API for ticket comments, every comment entry includes metadata about whether the comment was sent through the web portal or email or whatever, and potentially things like the user agent string and location of the browser where the person typed their comment. Could be useful for something, I guess, but not for answering the kinds of questions I'm asking. So we can cut it.
:::

## Best practices {.center}

### 3. Sanitize sensitive data

`n***@posit.co`

:::{.notes}
Finally, thinking back to the lethal trifecta, or even just good data goverance hygiene. If there are personally identifying details in the data you're pulling in, and you don't need them to answer your questions, you can either prune them entirely or redact them. 

In this example, we can keep the information that a user from Posit reported this issue, which could be useful--maybe I want to look up other issues reported by this company--but the personal identity does not leak out.
:::

## We have scorch'd the snake, not kill'd it {.center .folio background-color="#f5efe1"}

### [space]{.ghost}

::: {.notes}
Macbeth, and it's the honest caveat on everything I just said.

These practices shrink what you're exposed to. They don't make an agent safe, and I don't want anybody leaving here thinking that a small tool surface is the same thing as a trust boundary.

Which is the other half of the answer, and it's not in your server code. It's in where the thing runs.
:::

REPLACE ME with a real transcript before the talk -- the tool calls are
real (`get_ticket`, `list_ticket_comments`) but the ticket and the
diagnosis here are invented.

Same prompt as Act I. Same ticket. This time it just goes and reads it.

Two things worth pointing at on the way past: it took two tool calls, not twenty, because those are the only tools I gave it. And look at the requester line -- `n***@posit.co`. That's the third best practice, doing its job, in the middle of the answer.
:::

## Deployed on Posit Connect

* **Authentication** — a Zendesk OAuth integration, so the credentials live in Connect. Not in the agent, not in my `.env`

* **Hosting** — the server runs somewhere that can actually reach Zendesk

* **Monitoring** — I can see what it did, and who asked

* **Distribution** — `claude mcp add --transport http zendesk https://connect.example.com/zendesk/mcp`

:::{.notes}
This is where the three things a CLI couldn't do get done, and none of them are in my server code.

The auth one is the one I'd underline. Connect has a Zendesk OAuth integration, so the server picks up credentials from the logged-in user's OAuth session. There's no API token in an env var, and there's nothing for the agent to leak, because the agent never had it. That's an ingredient removed from the cauldron rather than a rule about not stirring it.

And the last line is the whole distribution story: colleagues don't install anything or get their own token. They get a URL.
:::

## MCP, or not MCP?

* MCP is (just) an API standard for AI agents

* Writing and deploying your own remote MCP servers can unlock superpowers for your agentic workflows

* AI brings inherent security risks, but a well designed MCP server can mitigate them

* You (or your agent) can easily write custom MCP servers
